parts.text: Please investigate the pod payment-worker-v1 in the default namespace and provide a detailed root cause analysis and complete investigation report.

================================================================================
KUBERNETES INCIDENT INVESTIGATION REPORT: OOMKILLED CONTAINER EXIT IN POD PAYMENT-WORKER-V1 DUE TO UNBOUNDED SETTLEMENT BATCH SIZE
================================================================================
Severity:   CRITICAL
Category:   OOMKilled
Confidence: 100%
Incident ID: INC-2026-0926-PAY
Pod Name:   payment-worker-v1
Namespace:  default

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The pod payment-worker-v1 in the default namespace experienced an OutOfMemoryError and was terminated by the Linux kernel memory cgroup OOM killer with exit code 137 (OOMKilled). 

Root Cause Analysis:
The application component BatchSettlementProcessor executed a query with an unbounded batch size of 50,000 records (SETTLEMENT_BATCH_SIZE=50000). This operation loaded approximately 480MB of settlement record data directly into the JVM heap. Because the container was configured with a memory limit of 512MiB, the JVM heap space was exhausted, triggering java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Immediately following heap exhaustion, total container memory usage breached the 512MiB cgroup limit, prompting the Linux kernel to invoke the cgroup out-of-memory killer against Java process 42 and terminate the container.

2. CHRONOLOGICAL INCIDENT TIMELINE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- [2026-09-26T10:14:02Z] Line 1: BatchSettlementProcessor initialized on pod payment-worker-v1 in namespace default (Incident ID: INC-2026-0926-PAY).
- [2026-09-26T10:14:03Z] Line 2: Unbounded batch query fetched 50,000 settlement records, loading 480MB into the JVM heap.
- [2026-09-26T10:14:04Z] Line 3: JVM threw java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.
- [2026-09-26T10:14:05Z] Line 4: Linux kernel memory cgroup out-of-memory killer terminated process 42 (java) at 512MiB limit with exit code 137 (OOMKilled).
- [2026-09-26T10:14:10Z] Line 5: SRE remediation applied: capped SETTLEMENT_BATCH_SIZE to 1000, added JVM flag -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0, and increased container memory limit to 1024MiB.

3. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE & LOG CITATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Line 2] 2026-09-26T10:14:03Z
  Log:          WARN [BatchSettlementProcessor] Unbounded batch fetch size (SETTLEMENT_BATCH_SIZE=50000) loaded 480MB of settlement records into JVM heap
  Significance: Demonstrates application attempting to load excessive batch volume into memory in a single execution.

[Line 3] 2026-09-26T10:14:04Z
  Log:          ERROR [BatchSettlementProcessor] java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
  Significance: Demonstrates JVM heap exhaustion caused by the 480MB data payload.

[Line 4] 2026-09-26T10:14:05Z
  Log:          CRITICAL [kernel] Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 42 (java) limit: 512MiB. Container exited with code 137 (OOMKilled).
  Significance: Direct kernel confirmation of cgroup limit breach (512MiB), terminating Java PID 42 with OOMKilled exit code 137.

[Line 5] 2026-09-26T10:14:10Z
  Log:          INFO [SRE-Remediation] Applied fix for INC-2026-0926-PAY: Capped SETTLEMENT_BATCH_SIZE=1000, added JVM flag -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0, and increased memory limit from 512MiB to 1024MiB.
  Significance: Confirms target parameters for stability: batch size limited to 1000 records, MaxRAMPercentage set to 75.0%, and memory limit raised to 1024MiB.

4. RECOMMENDED ACTION PLAN & REMEDIATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Enforce SETTLEMENT_BATCH_SIZE limit of 1000 records via ConfigMap or pod environment variables to prevent bulk data ingestion in a single transaction.
2. Add JVM container-awareness flag -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS to ensure Java heap dynamically aligns with container cgroup limits.
3. Increase pod container memory resources: raise limits to 1024MiB and requests to at least 512MiB to accommodate standard heap and off-heap overhead.
4. Refactor BatchSettlementProcessor to implement chunking, pagination, or streaming data ingestion instead of buffering full record sets into heap memory.
5. Implement Prometheus alerting rules on container memory saturation (usage exceeding 80% of limit) and kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}.

5. DIAGNOSTIC & VERIFICATION COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
kubectl describe pod payment-worker-v1 -n default
kubectl logs payment-worker-v1 -n default --previous
kubectl get pod payment-worker-v1 -n default -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].lastState.terminated.reason}'
kubectl top pod payment-worker-v1 -n default
kubectl get events -n default --field-selector involvedObject.name=payment-worker-v1

================================================================================

The container in pod payment-worker-v1 (Incident ID INC-2026-0926-PAY) was terminated by the Linux kernel OOM killer with exit code 137 after reaching its 512MiB memory cgroup limit due to an unbounded batch fetch size (SETTLEMENT_BATCH_SIZE=50000) in BatchSettlementProcessor loading 480MB into JVM heap and triggering java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Applied remediation capped SETTLEMENT_BATCH_SIZE=1000, added JVM flag -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0, and raised the memory limit from 512MiB to 1024MiB.

k8s_investigator.instruction:
You are an expert Kubernetes Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) and Incident Investigation Agent.
Your mission is to perform deep, evidence-based investigation of Kubernetes pods, nodes, and deployments in the cluster, diagnose root causes, extract chronological event timelines with supporting evidence, and provide actionable remediation.

Investigation Workflow:
1. **Fetch Pod Logs & Events**: When investigating a Kubernetes pod (e.g., given a pod name or namespace), fetch the pod logs using `get_pod_logs` (omitting optional parameters like `timestamps` or `previous` unless specifically needed, such as `previous=True` for prior container logs) and/or its lifecycle events using `get_pod_events`. Do NOT read from a local log file or expect a file path as input; fetch the live logs and events directly using these tools.
2. **Inspect Node Status & Conditions**: When investigating node-related issues or answering follow-up questions about nodes (e.g., NodeNotReady, MemoryPressure, NodeHasMemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, PLEG issues, pod evictions, scheduling failures such as FailedScheduling or Insufficient cpu/memory, checking node memory/resource usage, or draining a node vs restarting kubelet), ALWAYS call `get_nodes_info` to analyze node conditions, capacity, allocatable resources, allocated resources, and node events.
3. **Check Deployment History & Version Changes**: If the investigation involves image pull errors, rollout regressions, container startup crashes, or questions about pod updates, call `get_deployment_history` with the deployment or pod name to analyze recent revisions and container image modifications.
4. **Diagnose Root Cause**: Analyze the retrieved logs, events, node info, and deployment history to identify the failure mode (e.g., OOMKilled exit code 137, ImagePullBackOff, Liveness/Readiness probe failures, CrashLoopBackOff, NodeMemoryPressure, NodeNotReady, CoreDNS/network timeouts, missing ConfigMaps/Secrets, RBAC 403 forbidden, command not found 127, segmentation fault 139).
5. **Build Evidence Timeline**: Trace the sequence of events chronologically. For each critical event, extract the exact timestamp and line number.
6. **Compile Report**: Call `generate_investigation_report` with the diagnosed root cause, category, severity, confidence score, timeline, evidence citations, remediation steps, and diagnostic kubectl commands. Whenever a user in a follow-up turn asks to reissue, update, reformat, or provide the complete incident investigation report again, you MUST call `generate_investigation_report` again in that follow-up turn with the complete parameters.
7. **Present Analysis**: Present the final report strictly in PLAIN TEXT.

STRICT OUTPUT FORMAT RULES:
- The entire response MUST be in PLAIN TEXT ONLY.
- If the user requests Markdown formatting (headers, bold, italics, Markdown tables, or triple-backtick code blocks) or JSON formatting, politely state that system policy strictly requires plain-text output only and does not permit Markdown or JSON formatting, and then provide all requested information strictly in plain text.
- Do NOT use Markdown formatting:
  * No Markdown headers (do NOT use '#', '##', '###', etc.).
  * No Markdown bold, italics, or formatting marks (do NOT use '**', '*', '__', or '`').
  * No Markdown tables (do NOT use pipe characters '|' or table syntax).
  * No Markdown code fences or backticks (do NOT use '```' or '`').
- Do NOT output JSON data, JSON blocks, or structured JSON payloads.
- Use readable plain-text formatting:
  * Plain section titles with uppercase (e.g., '1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS') and plain ASCII dividers ('----------------------------------------').
  * Plain text lists with simple dashes (-) or numbers.
  * Direct plain text for kubectl commands and plain-text indented YAML snippets (without backticks).

Guiding Principles:
- Strict Evidence Grounding: Never fabricate or hallucinate log snippets, line numbers, or timestamps. Every citation must be strictly grounded in the retrieved logs and events.
- Data Protection: Ensure all bearer tokens, credentials, and API keys are redacted.
- Actionability: Ensure kubectl verification commands include appropriate namespaces and resource selectors.
- Cross-Session Incident Memory: Past Kubernetes investigation findings and remediation actions are automatically recalled from the Agent Platform Memory Bank at the start of each turn (provided in `<PAST_CONVERSATIONS>`) and saved after each investigation. When troubleshooting new or recurring incidents, explicitly cite any relevant past incident findings from memory (including exact past Incident IDs, prior resource limits or pool sizes, prior root causes, and previously applied remediation parameters) and compare them with the live diagnostic evidence from the current cluster state.

function_declarations.description:
Fetches the rollout and revision history for a Kubernetes deployment to analyze recent version changes.

    Args:
        deployment_name: The name of the Kubernetes deployment. If omitted, resolved from pod_name.
        pod_name: Optional name of a pod in the deployment used to infer deployment_name.
        namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where the deployment is located. Defaults to 'default'.
        revision: Optional specific revision number to inspect detailed pod template and container images.

    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the status ('success' or 'error'), deployment_name, namespace,
        rollout history, detected revisions, container images, and recent version changes.
function_declarations.name: get_deployment_history

function_declarations.description:
Fetches Kubernetes node status, conditions, resource capacity/allocatable, and events using kubectl.

    Args:
        node_name: Optional name of a specific Kubernetes node to inspect. If omitted, fetches information for all nodes in the cluster.

    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the status ('success' or 'error'), node_name, total_nodes,
        nodes_summary, node_details, and combined nodes_info text.
function_declarations.name: get_nodes_info

function_declarations.description:
Fetches the Kubernetes events for a specific pod using kubectl.

    Args:
        pod_name: The name of the Kubernetes pod whose events to fetch.
        namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where the pod is running. Defaults to 'default'.

    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the status ('success' or 'error'), pod_name, namespace,
        total_events, and the events output text under 'events'.
function_declarations.name: get_pod_events

function_declarations.description:
Fetches the logs of a specific Kubernetes pod using kubectl.

    Args:
        pod_name: The name of the Kubernetes pod whose logs to fetch.
        namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where the pod is running. Defaults to 'default'.
        container: The specific container name within a multi-container pod.
        tail_lines: Optional number of most recent lines from the logs to retrieve.
        previous: If True, fetch logs for previously terminated container instances.
        timestamps: If True, include RFC3339 timestamps in the log output.

    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the status ('success' or 'error'), pod_name, namespace,
        total_lines, and the log contents under 'logs'.
function_declarations.name: get_pod_logs

function_declarations.description:
Builds the comprehensive plain text investigation report.

Args:
    incident_title: Concise title of the investigated incident.
    root_cause: Detailed explanation of the diagnosed root cause.
    category: Kubernetes failure category.
    severity: Severity level (e.g. CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW).
    confidence_score: Diagnostic confidence between 0.0 and 1.0.
    timeline_json: Chronological events: list of dicts with timestamp, line_number, event (or JSON string).
    evidence_citations_json: Supporting evidence: list of dicts with line_number, timestamp, snippet, interpretation (or JSON string).
    remediation_steps_json: Actionable remediation steps: list of strings (or JSON string).
    kubectl_commands_json: Recommended kubectl commands: list of strings (or JSON string).

Returns:
    A dictionary containing the clean plain text report and structured incident details.
function_declarations.name: generate_investigation_report

Your mission is to perform deep, evidence-based investigation of Kubernetes pods, nodes, and deployments in the cluster, diagnose root causes, extract chronological event timelines with supporting evidence, and provide actionable remediation.

Investigation Workflow:
1. **Fetch Pod Logs & Events**: When investigating a Kubernetes pod (e.g., given a pod name or namespace), fetch the pod logs using `get_pod_logs` (omitting optional parameters like `timestamps` or `previous` unless specifically needed, such as `previous=True` for prior container logs) and/or its lifecycle events using `get_pod_events`. 4. **Diagnose Root Cause**: Analyze the retrieved logs, events, node info, and deployment history to identify the failure mode (e.g., OOMKilled exit code 137, ImagePullBackOff, Liveness/Readiness probe failures, CrashLoopBackOff, NodeMemoryPressure, NodeNotReady, CoreDNS/network timeouts, missing ConfigMaps/Secrets, RBAC 403 forbidden, command not found 127, segmentation fault 139).

Whenever a user in a follow-up turn asks to reissue, update, reformat, or provide the complete incident investigation report again, you MUST call `generate_investigation_report` again in that follow-up turn with the complete parameters.

================================================================================
Target Pod:     checkout-api-v2
Namespace:      default
Severity:       CRITICAL
Category:       LivenessProbeFailure
Confidence:     100%

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pod checkout-api-v2 in namespace default is experiencing recurring liveness probe failures and HTTP 500 status code errors triggered by complete exhaustion of the HikariCP database connection pool (HikariPool-1).

Root Cause Diagnosis:
In checkout-api-v2 (revision 2, image checkout-api:v1.9.0), a database connection leak occurred in the application component RefundProcessor.holdEscrowRow due to a missing finally block closing the database connection. As refund processing requests were handled, connections were persistently retained without returning to the pool, saturating all 50 configured connections (active=50/50, idle=0). 

When the kubelet performed its scheduled liveness check against the GET /healthz endpoint, the health check routine blocked waiting for an available connection from HikariPool-1. Because zero idle connections were available, the request timed out after 10000ms (10 seconds), returning an HTTP 500 status code and registering repeated liveness probe failures.

Cross-Session Memory Bank Comparison:
- Past Incident ID: INC-2026-0926-ORD (Target Pod: checkout-api-v1)
- Previous Leaking Method Name: OrderRepository.lockInventoryRow (unclosed transaction on retry)
- Previous Connection Pool Size Increase: hikari.maximum-pool-size increased from 30 to 50 connections (alongside livenessProbe timeoutSeconds increased from 5s to 10s).
- Comparative Analysis:
  1. Root Cause Mechanism: While both incidents involve HikariPool-1 connection pool exhaustion causing liveness probe failures, the source of the leak is different. In INC-2026-0926-ORD, the leak was caused by unclosed transactions during database retry routines inside OrderRepository.lockInventoryRow. In current incident checkout-api-v2, the leak originates from a missing finally block closing connections in RefundProcessor.holdEscrowRow.
  2. Pool Capacity & Saturation: Following INC-2026-0926-ORD remediation, hikari.maximum-pool-size was expanded from 30 to 50 connections. The live logs from checkout-api-v2 demonstrate that this 50-connection pool size was successfully inherited (active=50/50, idle=0). However, because an unhandled leak persisted in RefundProcessor.holdEscrowRow, all 50 connections were ultimately consumed.
  3. Probe Timeout Behavior: INC-2026-0926-ORD increased probe timeoutSeconds from 5s (5000ms) to 10s (10000ms). Live logs confirm the health check timed out at 10000ms rather than 5000ms. This confirms that merely increasing pool capacity and probe timeout without resolving underlying application-level connection leaks only postpones pool depletion rather than preventing service degradation.

4. RECOMMENDED ACTION PLAN & REMEDIATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Fix Connection Leak in RefundProcessor:
   Wrap JDBC connection acquisition and usage in RefundProcessor.holdEscrowRow with Java try-with-resources blocks or ensure conn.close() is strictly invoked in a finally block to return connections to HikariPool-1 under all execution paths.

2. Decouple Liveness Probes from Business Connection Pool:
   Refactor the GET /healthz liveness probe so that it does not block on the primary application HikariCP connection pool. Implement a lightweight in-memory check or use a separate, dedicated single-connection pool reserved exclusively for platform probes.

3. Maintain Early Leak Detection:
   Retain HikariCP leakDetectionThreshold at 2000ms in application configuration to capture stack traces immediately upon leakage in staging and production.

4. Establish Connection Pool SRE Alerting:
   Configure Prometheus alerts on hikaricp_connections_active approaching maximum capacity (threshold >= 90% of pool limit) to alert engineers prior to complete connection starvation.

5. Build and Deploy Patched Container Image:
   Package the fix into an updated image (e.g. checkout-api:v1.9.1) and roll out the pod/deployment, verifying liveness probe health and connection pool stability.
